newsitem.title: JAPAN: Former Japanese copper trader admits forgery.
newsitem.headline: Former Japanese copper trader admits forgery.

text.p: The former star trader of the world copper market, Yasuo Hamanaka, has admitted he forged documents relating to Sumitomo Corp.'s multibillion-dollar trading losses, one of his lawyers said Tuesday.
"At this time Hamanaka is admitting that he committed forgery, as charged by the Tokyo prosecutors' office," Hidesato Sekine, one of a team of three lawyers representing Hamanaka, told Reuters.
Hamanaka was arrested by prosecutors last week after Sumitomo, a giant trading house, filed a complaint that he forged documents authorising him to engage in certain copper trades.
Sumitomo has also blamed Hamanaka for racking up estimated losses of $2.6 billion from unauthorised copper trading, leading to the world's biggest-ever loss on financial markets.
While acknowledging guilt on the forgery counts, Hamanaka denied he manipulated world copper markets, concocted fictitious trades, or received any personal benefit from his transactions, Sekine said.
"He said he acted only for the sake of the company," the lawyer said.
Hamanaka did not clearly indicate, however, whether any of his superiors at Sumitomo had been aware of his activities.
Asked whether Hamanaka's superiors had known about his actions, Sekine said: "He did not make a direct reference to that issue."
Sumitomo officials have repeatedly insisted Hamanaka was acting without superiors' knowledge when he amassed the huge losses.
Sekine said he has had two 30-minute meetings with Hamanaka at the Tokyo detention centre where he has been held since his arrest.
Before Sumitomo fired him in mid-June of this year, Hamanaka was considered the most influential and controversial player in the world copper market.

Many traders have speculated that he kept copper prices artificially high in recent years through skilful use of complex derivatives transactions and his iron grip on a large portion of copper stocks in London Metal Exchange warehouses.

In 1991, a U.S. trader, David Threlkeld, said Hamanaka sent him a letter asking him to confirm fictitious trades. The LME and U.S. and British authorities investigated the matter, but no action was taken against Sumitomo or Hamanaka at that time.

Some legal experts said any guilty plea by Hamanaka might make it harder for investigators in the United States and Britain, for instance, to pursue inquiries to satisfy themselves that no laws were broken by anyone else in the jurisdictions where copper is traded.
"I would see a plea of guilty as choking off part of the expose," said Michael Levi, professor of Criminology at the University of Wales at Cardiff.

"The moment you plead guilty you stop calling for evidence from any of the other parties and it will probably reduce the number of subpoenas unless there are civil actions going on alongside it," Levi said.
A Hamanaka admission that he forged documents might make it harder to prosecute anyone else on whom regulatory suspicion fell.
"The likeliest is that the defence may take the line that they were just as deceived by forgeries as anyone else," said Leonard Leigh, professor of criminal law at the London School of Economics.
